$comment: The CLOSED set of CONNECTOR PLUGIN distributions this repository may
publish, and the conformance every entry must have passed first.
`scripts/release_connector.py resolve` gates on it and fails closed, so
listing a connector is a reviewed diff rather than a dispatch-time string —
the doctrine of `.github/release-modules.json` and
`.github/release-adapters.json`, applied to a third shape.
## Why a THIRD file
A connector is neither of the two shapes already governed.
It is not a MODULE: it owns no `mod_*` schema, no migration lineage and no
`MIGRATION_OWNER_LEDGER` allocation. Its state lives in the control plane's
`mod_intg`, which `dotmac-integration` owns and a connector never writes
directly. The module lane would ask it for a `db_schema` to compare against
a manifest and a `kernel_floor` naming the release that allocated it, and
it has neither.
It is not a STATELESS PROTOCOL ADAPTER either, and this is the distinction
that earns the file. An adapter is a library a product CALLS: it is
verified by its public surface, and nothing else in the fleet has an
opinion about it. A connector is DISCOVERED and EXECUTED by a control
plane it never imports the caller of — it registers in the
`dotmac_integration.connectors` entry-point group, targets a versioned SPI,
and is loaded at boot by `dotmac_integration.discovery.discover`, which is
FAIL-CLOSED AS A SET: one malformed connector refuses the whole registry
rather than silently offering the rest. So a connector's release gate has
to answer a question neither other lane asks — 'does this distribution
satisfy the SPI contract?' — and the answer is a function call, not a
review comment: `dotmac_integration.conformance`.
Making the adapter lane's fields optional was rejected for the reason that
lane already records about the module lane: optionality is not scoped to
the package that needs it. Once `spi_range` and `connector_key` may be
absent, a connector whose entry-point registration was dropped in a bad
merge stops being refused and starts being treated as an adapter, its
conformance proof skipped rather than failed.
## A release PROFILE, not a new extraction classification
`connector-plugin` is the name of this RELEASE PROFILE and of the
architectural role. It is deliberately NOT an `EXTRACTION.toml`
classification, and a connector's dossier says
`classification = "stateless-protocol-adapter"` like any other
distribution a product does not install. Adding a fourth classification
would require amending ADR-0006 and the global validator for no gain — the
four properties that classification governs (no ModuleManifest, no
lineage, no ledger allocation, no persistence import) are exactly the four
a connector has, and inventing a synonym for them would put the same
package in two vocabularies at once.
The consequence has to be stated plainly, because it is the one thing a
reader could get wrong: THE CLASSIFICATION NO LONGER SEPARATES THIS LANE
FROM THE ADAPTER LANE. Both accept `stateless-protocol-adapter`, so the
classification check is a floor both lanes share rather than the thing
that distinguishes them. What distinguishes this lane is the set of
STRICTER requirements below — exactly one connector entry point, a
published Integration floor, connector-key consistency, installed-wheel
SPI conformance, and no persistence, secret material or private
retry/checkpoint engine. Those are checks the adapter lane does not make,
and they are why a connector cannot simply be released through it.
`tests/architecture/test_connector_release_policy.py` proves the point the
hard way: `dotmac-auth-oidc` carries the identical classification and is
still refused by this gate.
## What earns an entry
Five things, and every one of them is checked rather than asserted in
review. `scripts/release_connector.py` is where each is enforced:
1. CLASSIFICATION and LOCATION. `EXTRACTION.toml` says
`stateless-protocol-adapter`, read from the package and never trusted
from this file — that is what stops this lane becoming a way to
publish a stateful module while skipping the namespace, lineage and
dual-plane gates the module lane performs. And `package_dir` must
start with `packages/dotmac-connector-`: first-party connectors live
under Starter `packages/` as independently built, tested, versioned
and published distributions, and the prefix is ENFORCED rather than
conventional so a connector cannot be released from somewhere the
naming does not announce it.
2. DISCOVERY. The package registers exactly one entry point in the
`dotmac_integration.connectors` group, and the `connector_key` this
entry declares is the one its manifest declares. A key mismatch is
invisible until two connectors collide in a live registry.
3. CONFORMANCE. `assert_plugin_conforms` passes against the INSTALLED
bytes — not the source tree, because only one of the two gets
published. It subsumes `assert_connector_conforms`, so metadata and
executability are proved together: a distribution that declares a
capability it cannot hand back a handler for passes every metadata
check and fails at the first dispatch.
4. AN INSTALLABLE FLOOR. `integration_floor` names the earliest
`dotmac-integration` release whose SPI admits this connector — and it
must be a PUBLISHED one. `release-modules.json` already states the
rule for kernels: 'A floor naming an unpublished version cannot be
resolved by an installer, so it is not a floor at all.' Here it is
enforced rather than only written down: `resolve` refuses an
`integration_floor` with no release tag. This bites on every SPI bump:
the current connector may floor at registry-verified integration a10,
while a merely declared future release remains inadmissible.
5. NO SECRET SHAPE, no persistence, and no private retry/checkpoint
engine. A connector holds a reference to credential material (ADR-0024
section 7); it never holds the value, it declares no tables, and it does
not carry its own delivery-retry or feed-checkpoint machinery — that is
precisely the surface `docs/inventories/external-connector-sources.md`
is ratcheting OUT of products and into the control plane. A connector
rebuilding it locally would move the duplication rather than retire it.
## What an entry does NOT prove
Exactly what a module allowlist row does not prove, restated because a
connector is the shape most likely to be read as an endorsement of a
provider integration:
* NOT that a version was published. The row says the workflow MAY
publish. `docs/inventories/declared-publication-baseline.json` is where
publication is tracked, and the two are deliberately separate files
because they answer different questions.
* NOT that anything adopted it. Adoption is `EXTRACTION.toml`'s
`contract_consumers`, which counts real cutovers, and a release moves
neither it nor `status`.
* NOT that the provider works. Conformance is proved against the SPI with
no network and no credentials — deliberately, so an author's first
experience of the SPI is not a secrets problem. A connector can conform
perfectly and still be misconfigured against a live provider; that is
what the control plane's health and quarantine paths are for.
## Why the first entry is here
The Meta/WhatsApp ingress connector is listed with its implementation,
prebuilt conformance corpus, installed-wheel SPI proof and published
dotmac-integration 0.1.0a10 floor. This is the rule ADR-0026 section 8 set
for release eligibility: the entry lands WITH the proof, never ahead of it.
THIS OBJECT IS THE LOCK. `.github/workflows/release-connector.yml` exists
and is NOT the lock — a reader must not mistake an input option for
authorization. `resolve` reads this exact object before build and again
after protected-environment approval.
The workflow input is now an exact choice list matching this object.
`tests/architecture/test_connector_release_policy.py` keeps that UI layer
and the enforced policy in sync in both directions.
The conformance obligations every connector must satisfy, named as the
callables that enforce them. These are not documentation: the guard
resolves each name in the shipped kit, so a rename in
`dotmac-integration` fails here instead of leaving this policy pointing
at a contract that moved.
